title: A Day at the Beach
intro: In Class 2 Maths Chapter 1, A Day at the Beach, the topics are: Counting in Groups of Ten, tens and ones with blocks and strips, making 100 with ten strips, writing numbers as tens and ones, comparing two-digit numbers, making and ordering two-digit numbers, numbers for position (first, second, third), numbers as names: dates and labels. Read the short notes, check every book question with the NCERT solutions, practise the important questions and then try the 30-mark sample paper. All four PDFs are free to download.
topics: Counting in Groups of Ten
Counting one by one is slow and we lose count
Tens and Ones with Blocks and Strips
A block stick has 10 blocks and a ten strip has 10 units — each is one TEN
Making 100 with Ten Strips
10 ten strips joined together make a 100 units grid
Writing Numbers as Tens and Ones
Use a ▲ card for each group of ten and a ● card for each one
Comparing Two-Digit Numbers
To compare two numbers, look at the tens first — more tens means more
Making and Ordering Two-Digit Numbers
The tens card decides how big a number is
Numbers for Position (First, Second, Third)
Words like first, second, third (1st, 2nd, 3rd) tell position
Numbers as Names: Dates and Labels
Some numbers do not tell how many — they name

items: Counting one by one is slow and we lose count. Putting things in equal groups — best of all in groups of ten — makes counting quick: so many tens and some loose ones.
Count big collections in groups, not one by one
A full group of 10 is one ten; left-over things are loose ones
25 chikoos = 2 trays of ten and 5 loose chikoos

notes.h: Tens and Ones with Blocks and Strips
items: A block stick has 10 blocks and a ten strip has 10 units — each is one TEN. A number like 34 is 3 tens and 4 ones.
1 block stick = 1 ten strip = 10 ones
The tens digit tells the number of sticks or strips; the ones digit tells the loose ones
10 ten strips joined together make a 100 units grid. Any two groups of strips that together make 10 strips make 100 units: 70 + 30, 50 + 50, 40 + 60, 20 + 80.
10 ones = 1 ten; 10 tens = 100
Pairs of strips that make 10 strips make 100: 1 + 9, 2 + 8, 3 + 7, 4 + 6, 5 + 5

notes.h: Writing Numbers as Tens and Ones
items: Use a ▲ card for each group of ten and a ● card for each one. 3 tens and 1 one = 30 + 1 = 31; in a T O chart the tens digit goes under T and the ones digit under O.
Tens digit = number of tens; ones digit = number of ones
52 = 50 + 2 = 5 tens 2 ones
Say the number name: 52 is fifty-two, 27 is twenty-seven
To compare two numbers, look at the tens first — more tens means more. If the tens are the same, the one with more ones is more.
More tens → more
Same tens → more ones is more
The tens card decides how big a number is. The smallest two-digit number is 10 and the largest is 99. To arrange numbers in decreasing order, keep picking the largest one left.
Smallest two-digit number 10, largest 99 (with one card of each digit 0–9 the largest you can make is 98)
Largest from two digits: bigger digit at tens
Decreasing order: largest first
Words like first, second, third (1st, 2nd, 3rd) tell position. In a race we count positions from the finish line.
1st, 2nd, 3rd … tell position, not how many
In a race, count from the finish line

notes.h: Numbers as Names: Dates and Labels
items: Some numbers do not tell how many — they name. A date names a day of the month; a jersey, house or bus number names a person or thing.
Dates and labels are numbers used as names
The way we write numbers with 0 and 1–9 began in India
Wrong: 8 trays of chikoos means 8 chikoos. Right: Each tray holds 10, so 8 trays = 80 chikoos — count trays by tens
Wrong: A block stick is 1 block. Right: A block stick is 10 blocks — one ten
Wrong: 100 is 10 units. Right: 10 units is one ten; 100 is 10 TEN STRIPS
Wrong: 3 tens and 1 one is 4. Right: Each ▲ is 10, so 3 tens = 30 and 30 + 1 = 31
Wrong: 34 is more than 43 because 4 is bigger than 3 in the ones place. Right: Tens decide first: 4 tens (43) beat 3 tens (34)
Wrong: The smallest two-digit number is 01. Right: 0 at the tens place makes a one-digit number; the smallest two-digit number is 10

sol_items: Count the coconuts, boats, children and oranges in the ...: Count each kind from the picture.
How did you count them: In groups. It is quicker and we do not lose count.
How many necklaces of shells with 10 shells in eac: Count the necklaces in the picture; each has 10 shells.
Balloons: how many groups, how many in each group, how ...: Groups of 4 and 2 loose balloons (count the groups in the picture).
Bananas: how many bunches, how many in each bunch, how ...: Read from the picture.
Surbhi's bracelets and mother's necklaces: groups and s...: Both are 50 shells. Mother's groups of 10 are quicker to count.
imp_items: 3 plates have 5 laddoos on each plate. Count the laddoos in groups of 5.
4 bags hold 10 marbles in each bag. How many marbles in all?
47 pencils go in boxes of ten. How many full boxes and how many loose pencils?
4 boxes and 7 loose pencils
6 boxes of ten pencils and 3 loose pencils: how many pencils?
How many units are in 2 ten strips?
A 100 grid has 6 yellow ten strips. How many red ten strips fill it?
4 red ten strips

title: Shapes Around Us
intro: In Class 2 Maths Chapter 2, Shapes Around Us, the topics are: Solid Shapes Around Us, faces, edges and corners, counting faces, edges and corners. Read the short notes, check every book question with the NCERT solutions, practise the important questions and then try the 30-mark sample paper. All four PDFs are free to download.
topics: Solid Shapes Around Us
Objects around us have solid shapes: cube, cuboid, cylinder, cone and sphere
Faces, Edges and Corners
A solid shape has faces (its surfaces), edges (where faces meet) and corners (where edges meet)
Counting Faces, Edges and Corners
Box shapes have 6 flat faces, 12 edges and 8 corners; round shapes have fewer flat faces and few or no corners

items: Objects around us have solid shapes: cube, cuboid, cylinder, cone and sphere. Objects that look alike have the same shape.
Five solid shapes: cube, cuboid, cylinder, cone, sphere
Look at the object from all sides before naming its shape
A solid shape has faces (its surfaces), edges (where faces meet) and corners (where edges meet). A box has 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 corners.
Face = surface, Edge = line where faces meet, Corner = point where edges meet
Cube and cuboid: 6 faces, 12 edges, 8 corners
Box shapes have 6 flat faces, 12 edges and 8 corners; round shapes have fewer flat faces and few or no corners. We can sort objects by how many corners they have.
Corners: sphere 0, cylinder 0, cone 1, cube and cuboid 8
Box shapes: 6 flat faces, 12 edges, 8 corners
Flat faces: sphere 0, cone 1, cylinder 2
Wrong: Every round thing is a sphere — a drum is round, so it is a sphere. Right: A drum is round only at the top; from the side it is straight — it is a cylinder. A sphere is round from every side
Wrong: A box has 4 faces — the ones I can see. Right: Turn the box: top, bottom, front, back, left, right = 6 faces
Wrong: A cylinder has corners because it has edges. Right: Its 2 edges are round lines; no edges meet at a point, so it has 0 corners

sol_items: A(i). Circle the instruments similar in shape to a: Dholak, tabla and the big drums.
A(iv). How is the shape of a harmonium different from a...: A harmonium is a cuboid with flat faces and corners. A drum is a cylinder with a curved side and two round faces.
C row 1. Odd one out: carrot, ice-cream cone, orange, p...: Orange (a sphere)
C row 2. Odd one out: House (a cuboid)
C row 3. Odd one out: chalk, wooden box, layered sweet ...: Chalk (a cylinder)
Match the objects with the shapes: Drum, pencil - cylinder. Harmonium, chest - cuboid. Bell, cone, party horn - cone. Box drum, dice - cube. Matka, laddoo - sphere.
imp_items: Name the shape of a bell and of a globe.
A bell is a cone; a globe is a sphere.
Cross the odd one out: dice, matchbox, ball, brick.
Ball (it is a sphere; the other three are box shapes).
How many faces, edges and corners does a matchbox have?
6 faces, 12 edges and 8 corners.
Name two objects that have no corners.
Any two of: ball, orange, laddoo, chalk, drum, bottle.
How can you make an object with one face from clay?
Roll the clay into a ball; it has one round surface.

title: Fun with Numbers
intro: In Class 2 Maths Chapter 3, Fun with Numbers, the topics are: Counting up to 100 on a Ginladi, numbers on a number line, more than or less than: guess my number, steps forward and backward, adding two dice: bingo, skip counting forward, numbers common to two skips, skip counting backward, patterns in the number chart, number window: 1 more, 1 less, 10 more, 10 less, growing block patterns. Read the short notes, check every book question with the NCERT solutions, practise the important questions and then try the 30-mark sample paper. All four PDFs are free to download.
topics: Counting up to 100 on a Ginladi
A ginladi is a string of beads in coloured groups of ten
Numbers on a Number Line
On a number line the numbers stand in order with equal gaps
More Than or Less Than: Guess my Number
Every number is more than the numbers before it and less than the numbers after it
Steps Forward and Backward
A step forward goes to the next bigger number; a step backward goes to the number just before
Adding Two Dice: Bingo
Two dice give a sum from 2 to 12 (the Bingo grid uses only these numbers)
Skip Counting Forward
Skip counting forward is jumping the same number of steps each time
Numbers Common to Two Skips
Mark one skip count with one sign and another with a different sign on the same number chart; numbers with BOTH signs are common ...
Skip Counting Backward
Counting backward is jumping down by the same number of steps each time
Patterns in the Number Chart
The 1–100 chart has rows of ten
Number Window: 1 More, 1 Less, 10 More, 10 Less
Around any number in the 1–100 chart: the number above is 10 less, below is 10 more, left is 1 less and right is 1 more
Growing Block Patterns
Count the blocks in each shape and find how many are added each time; adding by the same rule extends the pattern

notes.h: Counting up to 100 on a Ginladi
items: A ginladi is a string of beads in coloured groups of ten. Count the groups of ten first, then the single beads, to know the number of any bead.
Each colour group = 10 beads
The whole ginladi = 10 groups of ten = 100 beads
Number = tens first, then ones
On a number line the numbers stand in order with equal gaps. Read the numbers at the two ends to know how much each gap is worth, then find any number.
Bigger numbers are to the right
Halfway between 60 and 70 is 65

notes.h: More Than or Less Than: Guess my Number
items: Every number is more than the numbers before it and less than the numbers after it. Yes/no questions like 'Is it more than 50?' cut away many numbers at once until only one is left.
A number on the right of the line is more
'Same digits' numbers: 11, 22, 33 … 99
A step forward goes to the next bigger number; a step backward goes to the number just before. Count the jumps, not the number you start on.
Forward = +1 each step, backward = 1 less each step
Two dice give a sum from 2 to 12 (the Bingo grid uses only these numbers). To find the sum, start at one die's number and step forward by the other (added).
Count on from the bigger number — fewer steps
Skip counting forward is jumping the same number of steps each time. Find how much the numbers go up, then keep adding the same jump.
Jump size = how much the numbers go up
Same jump each time = a pattern
Mark one skip count with one sign and another with a different sign on the same number chart; numbers with BOTH signs are common to both skips.
Check the bigger skip's numbers against the smaller skip — fewer to check
Counting backward is jumping down by the same number of steps each time. Find how much the numbers go down, then keep taking away the same jump.
Backward jump size = how much the numbers go down
The 1–100 chart has rows of ten. Numbers in one column end in the same digit, and the green diagonal goes up by 11 each time.
One row of the chart = 10 numbers
A column keeps the same ones digit

notes.h: Number Window: 1 More, 1 Less, 10 More, 10 Less
items: Around any number in the 1–100 chart: the number above is 10 less, below is 10 more, left is 1 less and right is 1 more.
Up −10, down +10, left −1, right +1
Count the blocks in each shape and find how many are added each time; adding by the same rule extends the pattern.
Check two gaps when you have three or more shapes; with only two shapes, look at how the picture grows
Wrong: Count every bead one by one from 1 to find 65. Right: Count by tens (10, 20 … 60), then 5 ones — faster and fewer mistakes
Wrong: Each mark on the line is 1 more. Right: Read the ends first, then count in tens from 20: 30, 40 … 80 lands exactly on the last mark — so each gap is 10
Wrong: Guess one number at a time: Is it 1? Is it 2? …. Right: Ask a more/less question — one answer throws away half the numbers
Wrong: Count the starting number as step 1 (52 to 58 = 7 steps). Right: The first jump lands on 53 — that is step 1, so 52 to 58 is 6 steps
Wrong: Write 1 or 13 on the Bingo grid. Right: Two dice give at least 2 and at most 12 — 1 and 13 never come
Wrong: Counting in twos from 10 will reach every number, like 43. Right: Twos from 10 land only on 10, 12, 14 … — numbers ending in 0, 2, 4, 6, 8

sol_items: C. Make cards 38, 44, 58, 65, 98 and place them on the ...: 38: 3 groups and 8 beads. 44: 4 and 4. 58: 5 and 8. 65: 6 and 5. 98: 9 and 8.
Write the numbers where the black, red and brown a: Black 30, red 50, brown 60.
Draw an ant on 65: Draw it halfway between 60 and 70.
Draw a sugar cube on 79: Draw it just before 80.
Jumpy the frog: Yes. The jumps are equal, so it is a pattern.
imp_items: A bead string has 10 groups of ten beads each. How many beads does it have?
A line goes from 10 to 70 with marks in tens. An ant sits on the 4th mark after 10. What number is it?
10, then 20, 30, 40, 50: the ant is on 50
On a line with marks 40, 50, 60, where do you draw 55 and 59?
55 halfway between 50 and 60; 59 just before 60 (1 less than 60)
A ladybird is on 61 and a leaf is on 67. How many steps forward?
A frog on 50 jumps 3 forward, 5 backward and 4 backward. Where does it reach?
Two dice show 2 and 6. Find the total by counting on.
start on 6, count on 2: 7, 8 → 8

title: Shadow Story
intro: In Class 2 Maths Chapter 4, Shadow Story, the topics are: Shadows and Shapes, tracing objects to get flat shapes, circle, rectangle, triangle and square, corners and edges: straight and curved, shape patterns, number patterns. Read the short notes, check every book question with the NCERT solutions, practise the important questions and then try the 30-mark sample paper. All four PDFs are free to download.
topics: Shadows and Shapes
A shadow forms when an object blocks light
Tracing Objects to Get Flat Shapes
When we keep an object's flat face on paper and draw around it, the line we get is a flat shape — the same shape as that face
Circle, Rectangle, Triangle and Square
Four flat shapes are all around us: circle (round), rectangle (4 sides, like a shoe box face), triangle (3 sides) and square (4 ...
Corners and Edges: Straight and Curved
Shapes have edges (border lines) and corners (where two straight edges meet)
Shape Patterns
A pattern is an arrangement that follows a rule: a part repeats, or changes, or turns the same way each time
Number Patterns
In a number pattern the same number is added each time (the same jump)

items: A shadow forms when an object blocks light. Its shape shows the outline of the object, and its size changes when the light moves.
Light + an object to block it → a shadow
The shadow has the outline (shape) of the object
Torch near → big shadow; far → small shadow
Sun high at noon → shortest shadow

notes.h: Tracing Objects to Get Flat Shapes
items: When we keep an object's flat face on paper and draw around it, the line we get is a flat shape — the same shape as that face.
Trace = draw around the face that touches the paper
Same face shape → same trace shape, even if sizes differ
Four flat shapes are all around us: circle (round), rectangle (4 sides, like a shoe box face), triangle (3 sides) and square (4 equal sides). Each can 'hide' in objects of its own shape.
Circle — round
Triangle — 3 sides
Rectangle — 4 sides, long and short
Square — 4 equal sides

notes.h: Corners and Edges: Straight and Curved
items: Shapes have edges (border lines) and corners (where two straight edges meet). Edges are straight or curved; an object with only curved edges has no corners.
Corner = where two edges meet
Only curved edges → 0 corners
Square: 4 corners, 4 edges; triangle: 3 corners, 3 edges
A pattern is an arrangement that follows a rule: a part repeats, or changes, or turns the same way each time. Find the rule and you can draw what comes next.
Find the rule before drawing
Repeat: find the part that comes again
Change: see what grows each time
Turn: see which way the shape turns
In a number pattern the same number is added each time (the same jump). Find the jump from the first two numbers and keep adding it.
Jump = how much from one number to the next
Add the same jump every time
Check: every gap must be the same
Wrong: A shadow stays even in a dark room. Right: No light → no shadow; the shadow vanishes when the light goes
Wrong: Two objects must be the same size to have the same trace shape. Right: A coin and a plate are different sizes but both trace a circle — shape, not size
Wrong: A square and a rectangle are the same shape. Right: Square: 4 equal sides. Rectangle: 2 long and 2 short sides
Wrong: A round table has corners too. Right: A round table has only a curved edge — 0 corners, so 'Catch the Corner' cannot be played
Wrong: Just copy the last shape to continue a pattern. Right: Find the rule first: a repeating part, a change, or a turn
Wrong: 1, 4 … next is 5 (just count on by 1). Right: The jump from 1 to 4 is 3, so next is 7

sol_items: How are these shadows (of the puppet play) forming: The puppet blocks the light, so a dark shadow shows on the screen.
Have you seen your own shadow or the shadow of a tree, ...: Yes (sample).
When do we see a shadow?: When an object blocks light.
When does a shadow vanish?: In the dark, at night, or when the light is not blocked.
Will the size of shadows change on changing the positio...: Yes. Torch near the object: big shadow. Torch far: small shadow.
At what time of the day is your shadow longest?: In the morning and in the evening.
imp_items: Name two objects that have the same trace as a coin.
A bangle and the bottom of a glass (any round-faced object, such as a button)
Circle wants to hide in the kitchen. Name two round things where it can hide.
A plate and a round roti (any two round-faced things)
A rectangle table has 4 children at its corners and one child in the middle of a short side. Who is out and claps next?
The child in the middle of the short side, because that place is not a corner
Is the edge of a roti straight or curved? And the edge of a notebook?
Roti: curved edge. Notebook: straight edges
How many corners and how many edges does a door have?
4 corners and 4 edges
Extend: circle, square, circle, square, circle, ___, ___.
square, circle

title: Playing with Lines
intro: In Class 2 Maths Chapter 5, Playing with Lines, the topics are: Standing, Sleeping and Slanting Lines, straight and curved lines, drawing shapes and designs with lines. Read the short notes, check every book question with the NCERT solutions, practise the important questions and then try the 30-mark sample paper. All four PDFs are free to download.
topics: Standing, Sleeping and Slanting Lines
A thread held tight makes a straight line
Straight and Curved Lines
When the thread is loose (hands brought closer), it bends and makes a curved line — a curved line is not straight
Drawing Shapes and Designs with Lines
Straight lines join dots into shapes; curved lines make clouds and rainbows; mixing types makes designs

items: A thread held tight makes a straight line. A straight line can stand (vertical), sleep (horizontal) or slant (tilted) — all three are straight.
Tight thread = straight line
Standing = vertical, sleeping = horizontal, slanting = tilted
Standing, sleeping and slanting lines are all straight
When the thread is loose (hands brought closer), it bends and makes a curved line — a curved line is not straight. We can find all four lines around us.
Loose thread = curved line
Curved line bends; straight line does not
A picture can have all four lines: standing, sleeping, slanting, curved

notes.h: Drawing Shapes and Designs with Lines
items: Straight lines join dots into shapes; curved lines make clouds and rainbows; mixing types makes designs. Folding paper is another way to make lines: a pressed fold gives a straight crease.
Straight lines join dots into shapes
Curved lines make clouds, rainbows, petals
Count the types of lines by naming each part's line once
A pressed fold of flat paper makes a straight crease
Wrong: A slanting line is not straight because it is tilted. Right: A slanting line is straight — the tight thread was tilted but did not bend
Wrong: A slanting line and a curved line are the same — both are not standing straight. Right: A slanting line is straight, only tilted; a curved line bends

Wrong: More lines means more types of lines (a house with 2 walls, a floor, a roof and a sun has 5 types). Right: Count each way of going only once: standing, sleeping, slanting, curved — that house has 4 types

sol_items: C. Cross the aasanas which have curved lines: Back-bend and cobra-like poses.
D. Put a star on the aasanas with sleeping or horizonta...: The child lying flat on the ground.
Trace the missing vertical, horizontal, slanting and cu...: Standing: lamp post, swing poles. Sleeping: top bars. Slanting: slide, see-saw. Curved: arch climber, round frames.
B. Try to make curved lines by paper folding: The edge of a round paper folded in half, or a card bent without pressing, shows curves.
imp_items: Which line does a ladder leaning on a wall make?
A slanting line
A child stands with arms stretched out to the sides. Which two lines does the pose have?
A standing line (the body) and sleeping lines (the arms)
Is the edge of a bangle straight or curved?
Curved
Name the line in each part of an umbrella: the stick and the top.
The stick is a straight standing line; the top is curved
Make a tent shape on dots. Which lines do you use?
Two slanting lines for the sides and one sleeping line on the ground
Draw a cloud on dots. What kind of lines make its edge?
Bumpy curved lines

subject: Maths
title: Decoration for Festival
intro: In Class 2 Maths Chapter 6, Decoration for Festival, the topics are: Adding Tens and Ones without Carrying, adding by counting ahead on ginladi and number line, adding with carrying (shifting the tens), addition word problems, subtracting by counting back on ginladi and number line, subtracting tens and ones without borrowing, subtracting with borrowing (opening a ten), subtraction word problems, addition and subtraction facts, addition and subtraction pyramids and diagrams, checking answers: spot the mistake. Read the short notes, check every book question with the NCERT solutions, practise the important questions and then try the 30-mark sample paper. All four PDFs are free to download.
topics: Adding Tens and Ones without Carrying
A garland is 10 flowers, so every number is garlands (tens) and loose flowers (ones)
Adding by Counting Ahead on Ginladi and Number Line
To add, start at the first number and count ahead
Adding with Carrying (Shifting the Tens)
When the ones add up to 10 or more, 10 ones make 1 ten
Addition Word Problems
When a story puts two groups together — 'together', 'in all', 'total', 'gifted more' — we add
Subtracting by Counting Back on Ginladi and Number Line
To take away, start at the bigger number and count back
Subtracting Tens and Ones without Borrowing
Take away ones from ones and tens from tens — ones first
Subtracting with Borrowing (Opening a Ten)
If the top ones are fewer than the ones to take away, open 1 ten into 10 ones
Subtraction Word Problems
Stories where things are given, sold, spent, burst or got down ask 'how many left' — take away
Addition and Subtraction Facts
Three numbers like 20, 30 and 50 make a fact family: two adding facts and two take-away facts
Addition and Subtraction Pyramids and Diagrams
In a number pyramid each box is the sum of the two boxes below it
Checking Answers: Spot the Mistake
Check every answer: tens under tens, shift a ten when ones make 10 or more, open a ten when top ones are fewer, and check a ...

notes.h: Adding Tens and Ones without Carrying
items: A garland is 10 flowers, so every number is garlands (tens) and loose flowers (ones). To add, put ones with ones and tens with tens.
1 garland = 10 flowers = 1 ten
Ones + ones, tens + tens
A number with 0 ones (20) still keeps its 0 in the ones place

notes.h: Adding by Counting Ahead on Ginladi and Number Line
items: To add, start at the first number and count ahead. On a ginladi we move beads; on a number line we jump — 10 at a time, then ones.
Start at the first number, count the second number ahead
Jump tens first, then ones
Number line = beads replaced by numbers
When the ones add up to 10 or more, 10 ones make 1 ten. Shift that ten to the tens place and add it with the tens.
10 ones = 1 ten
Ones first; if 10 or more, shift 1 ten
Tens + the shifted ten
When a story puts two groups together — 'together', 'in all', 'total', 'gifted more' — we add.
Read what is asked first
Two groups put together → add
Write the answer with its name (runs, ₹, people)

notes.h: Subtracting by Counting Back on Ginladi and Number Line
items: To take away, start at the bigger number and count back. On a number line jump back 10 at a time, then ones. Taking away 0 leaves the number; taking a number from itself leaves 0.
Start at the bigger number and count back
Jump back 10s first, then ones
Take away 0 → same number; take away itself → 0

notes.h: Subtracting Tens and Ones without Borrowing
items: Take away ones from ones and tens from tens — ones first. The number we start with goes on top.
Start number on top
Ones first, then tens
If the top ones are fewer than the ones to take away, open 1 ten into 10 ones. Then take away the ones, then the tens.
Top ones fewer? Open 1 ten
Opened ten: tens 1 less, ones 10 more
Then ones, then tens
Stories where things are given, sold, spent, burst or got down ask 'how many left' — take away. 'How many more to reach' and 'how many came' also take away: bigger number − smaller number.
Left after giving / selling / spending → take away
How many more to reach → bigger − smaller
Two things bought → add first, then take away
Three numbers like 20, 30 and 50 make a fact family: two adding facts and two take-away facts. The biggest number goes on top of the triangle (we call it the whole — added word).
Biggest number = the whole, on top (added word)
Part + part = whole (added words)
Whole − one part = the other part (added words)

notes.h: Addition and Subtraction Pyramids and Diagrams
items: In a number pyramid each box is the sum of the two boxes below it. When a top box is known, a missing box is found by taking away. In the corner diagram, the number between two corners is their sum.
Box = sum of the two below
Missing box = the box above − the other box below it
Check by adding again
Check every answer: tens under tens, shift a ten when ones make 10 or more, open a ten when top ones are fewer, and check a take-away by adding back.
Look at the ones first
Check a take-away by adding back: 18 + 17 = 35
Check an adding sum with the tens first: 2 tens + 3 tens = 5 tens, so 25 + 36 is in the 50s or 60s — never 511
Wrong: Add the tens of one number to the ones of the other (12 + 53 → 1 + 3 and 2 + 5). Right: Ones go with ones, tens with tens — write each digit in its own column
Wrong: Count the starting bead as step 1 (25 + 12 → stop at 36). Right: Start ON 25; the first step lands on 26, so 12 steps end at 37
Wrong: Write all of 13 in the answer: 36 + 47 = 713. Right: Only 3 ones stay; the 1 ten is shifted to the tens → 83
Wrong: A 2-digit sum cannot pass 99, so 43 + 58 = 91 (the shifted ten is dropped) or 11. Right: 3 + 8 = 11 → keep 1, shift 1 ten; 4 + 5 + 1 = 10 tens = 1 hundred, so 43 + 58 = 101
Wrong: Count the starting bead as the first step back (19 − 15 → stop at 5). Right: Start ON 19; the first step back lands on 18, so 15 steps end at 4
Wrong: 'Subtract 24 from 37' means 24 on top. Right: We start with 37, so 37 goes on top: 37 − 24 = 13

sol_items: Complete the garland table: Suwali 5 garlands 3 flowers = 53. Javed 4 garlands 3 flowers = 43. Zoha 2 garlands 0 flowers = 20.
Add these numbers: 67, 79, 85, 82
Rahim made 43 runs and 58 runs: runs in the two matches...: 43 + 58 = 101 runs
imp_items: Simran has 4 garlands and 6 loose flowers. How many flowers is that?
46 flowers (40 + 6)
32 + 6 on the ginladi: count 6 beads ahead of 32
46 + 27 by jumps of 10, then ones
From 31 the jumps are +10 and +7 and the end is 48. What number was added?

subject: Maths
title: Rani's Gift
intro: In Class 2 Maths Chapter 7, Rani's Gift, the topics are: Measuring with Handspans, measuring length and height with objects, longest and shortest path, heavier and lighter, comparing weights with a balance, measuring how much: glasses, spoons and bottles. Read the short notes, check every book question with the NCERT solutions, practise the important questions and then try the 30-mark sample paper. All four PDFs are free to download.
topics: Measuring with Handspans
We can measure length by counting handspans
Measuring Length and Height with Objects
Choose one object as the unit (textbook, block, eraser, pencil), place it end to end with no gaps, and count
Longest and Shortest Path
To find which path is longer, count its small equal pieces (or lay a thread along it and compare the thread)
Heavier and Lighter
We compare weight by lifting: one thing is heavier or lighter than another
Comparing Weights with a Balance
A balance compares two weights: the side with the heavier thing goes down, the lighter side goes up, and level means the same ...
Measuring How Much: Glasses, Spoons and Bottles
How much a drink needs or a bottle holds is counted in units like glasses, spoons and pinches

items: We can measure length by counting handspans. But hands are of different sizes, so the same bed can be 10, 8 or 14 handspans — to agree, everyone must use one same measure.
Big unit → small count; small unit → big count
To agree on a length, everyone must use one same measure

notes.h: Measuring Length and Height with Objects
items: Choose one object as the unit (textbook, block, eraser, pencil), place it end to end with no gaps, and count. Guess (estimate) first, then measure to check. Height is measured the same way, going up.
Start at the edge, no gaps, no overlaps, count
Guess first, then measure
Height is length going up
To find which path is longer, count its small equal pieces (or lay a thread along it and compare the thread). The path with the most pieces is the longest; the one with the fewest is the shortest.
Count the equal pieces or use a thread
Most pieces = longest; fewest = shortest
Fast way to school = shortest path

We compare weight by lifting: one thing is heavier or lighter than another. In a group, one is the heaviest and one is the lightest, and we can arrange things from lightest to heaviest. Big size does not always mean heavy.
Heavier/lighter for two things; heaviest/lightest for a group
If A is heavier than B, then B is lighter than A
Size does not tell weight — lift it
A balance compares two weights: the side with the heavier thing goes down, the lighter side goes up, and level means the same weight. Many light things can balance one heavy thing.
Down = heavier, up = lighter, level = same
Many light things can balance one heavy thing
Check the balance is level when empty

notes.h: Measuring How Much: Glasses, Spoons and Bottles
items: How much a drink needs or a bottle holds is counted in units like glasses, spoons and pinches. For 3 glasses of nimbu pani, every ingredient is taken 3 times. Bottles are compared by counting how many glasses fill them.
Count how much in glasses, spoons, pinches
For 3 glasses take each amount 3 times
More glasses to fill = holds more
Wrong: The carpenter cheated or the bed shrank. Right: The bed is the same; the carpenter's hand is smaller than the raja's, so 10 of his handspans are shorter than 10 of the raja's
Wrong: Gaps between the units do not matter. Right: Each unit must start where the last one ended — gaps or overlaps give a wrong count
Wrong: Paths with the same number of turns are the same length. Right: Path 1 and path 2 both turn 5 times but have 6 and 8 sides — count the sides, not the turns
Wrong: A bigger thing is always heavier. Right: Same-size bags: sand is heavier than dry leaves; a big balloon is very light
Wrong: The side that goes up is the heavier side. Right: The heavier side goes DOWN; the lighter side goes up
Wrong: For 3 glasses, only the water is made 3 times. Right: Every ingredient is taken once for each glass — sugar, lemon juice and salt too

sol_items: Why did the same bed measure 10, 8 and 14 handspans? Wh...: A bigger hand gives a smaller count. Everyone should use one same measure, for example the raja's own handspan or a fixed object.
Which path should Kavita take to reach school fast: The shorter bottom road, not the looping top road.
Choose the longest path from A to B in the three g: Path 1 has 6 sides, path 2 has 8, path 3 has 10. Path 3 is the longest.
Make the shortest path between A and B: The shortest path needs 6 sides (3 across and 3 down).
Discuss: We cannot tell by looking. Lift them or use a balance.
Make your own balance with cups, thread and a hang: The cup that goes down has the heavier object.
imp_items: A pencil box is laid end to end along a table with no gaps and fits 6 times. Write the length of the table.
6 pencil boxes (number + unit)
Meena's table is 6 of her handspans long; her father counts 4 handspans for the same table. Whose hand is bigger?
Her father's: a bigger hand gives a smaller count
Path P has 5 sides, path Q has 7 sides, path R has 4 sides. Which is the longest and which is the shortest?
Q is the longest; R is the shortest
A book is heavier than a pencil. Say it the other way round.
The pencil is lighter than the book
An eraser, a notebook and a school bag: arrange them from lightest to heaviest and name the heaviest.
eraser, notebook, school bag; the school bag is the heaviest
On a balance the left pan goes up and the right pan goes down. Which pan has the heavier thing?
The right pan (the side that goes down)

subject: Maths
title: Grouping and Sharing
intro: In Class 2 Maths Chapter 8, Grouping and Sharing, the topics are: Equal Groups and Times (×), tables of 2, 3, 5 and 10, making a new table from two tables, same total either way, word problems on equal groups, sharing equally, how many groups?. Read the short notes, check every book question with the NCERT solutions, practise the important questions and then try the 30-mark sample paper. All four PDFs are free to download.
topics: Equal Groups and Times (×)
When every group has the same number, we do not need to add again and again: 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 8 is '4 times 2', '4 groups of 2', ...
Tables of 2, 3, 5 and 10
A table writes the × facts of one number in order
Making a New Table from Two Tables
Add two tables row by row and you get a new table: table of 2 + table of 2 = table of 4; 3 + 3 → 6; 3 + 4 → 7; 2 + 6 → 8
Same Total Either Way
4 groups of 3 and 3 groups of 4 are different groups, but the total is the same: 4 × 3 = 3 × 4 = 12
Word Problems on Equal Groups
In a story, find how many groups and how many in EACH group; total = groups × number in each
Sharing Equally
Sharing equally means every group gets the same number
How Many Groups?
When we know the total and how many go in each group, we make groups of that size one after another until nothing is left, and ...

items: When every group has the same number, we do not need to add again and again: 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 8 is '4 times 2', '4 groups of 2', '4 twos are 8', written 4 × 2 = 8.
Equal groups: every group has the same number
4 times 2 = 4 groups of 2 = 4 twos = 4 × 2 = 8
First number: how many groups · second number: how many in each
A table writes the × facts of one number in order. Each row has one more in every group, so the answers of the table of 2 go up by 2, of 3 by 3, of 5 by 5, of 10 by 10.
Table of 2 goes up by 2, of 3 by 3, of 5 by 5, of 10 by 10
Table of 5 answers end in 5 or 0
Table of 10 answers end in 0

notes.h: Making a New Table from Two Tables
items: Add two tables row by row and you get a new table: table of 2 + table of 2 = table of 4; 3 + 3 → 6; 3 + 4 → 7; 2 + 6 → 8.
Two tables added column by column make a new table
The new table's number = the two numbers added (3 + 4 = 7)
Check the first column: 3 + 4 = 7 is the first number of the table of 7
4 groups of 3 and 3 groups of 4 are different groups, but the total is the same: 4 × 3 = 3 × 4 = 12. Turn an arrangement around and the total does not change.
Turn the picture round: rows become columns, the total stays
If you know one fact, you know its turn-around fact
In a story, find how many groups and how many in EACH group; total = groups × number in each. The word 'each' points to the number in one group.
Find: how many groups? how many in each?
Total = groups × each
Write the unit in the answer: bindis, buttons, ₹, people
Sharing equally means every group gets the same number. Give 1 to each group again and again until nothing is left; then count one group. Check: groups × each = total.
Share 1 by 1 until none are left
Equal: every group gets the same number
Check: groups × each = total
When we know the total and how many go in each group, we make groups of that size one after another until nothing is left, and count the groups: 20 beads, 5 in each bracelet → 4 bracelets.
Make groups of the given size until none are left
Count the groups
Check: groups × each = total
Wrong: 4 × 2 means 4 + 2 = 6. Right: 4 × 2 means 4 groups of 2: 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 8
Wrong: Each next row of a table adds 1. Right: Each next row adds the table's number: table of 3 → 3, 6, 9, 12
Wrong: Add numbers from different places, like the 2nd of one table and the 3rd of the other. Right: Add numbers that stand in the same column (same row number)
Wrong: 4 groups of 3 and 3 groups of 4 give different totals. Right: Both give 12; only the groups look different
Wrong: Add the two numbers in the story (8 packets, 5 bindis → 13). Right: 8 groups of 5 = 8 × 5 = 40, not 8 + 5
Wrong: Sharing 24 bananas among 3 monkeys gives 3 bananas each. Right: 3 is the number of monkeys; give out all 24 → 8 each

sol_items: Ramya says 7 cars with 4 wheels each have 7 times 4 = 2...: 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 = 28, so 7 times 4 = 28.
Cars: number of cars, wheels in each, total, times, gro...: 7 cars, 4 wheels each. 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 = 28; 7 times 4 = 28; 7 groups of 4; 7 x 4 = 28. We add seven fours.
Butterflies: 2 + 2 + 2 = 6; 3 groups of 2; 3 times 2 = 6; 3 twos; 3 x 2 = 6.
Octopuses: 8 + 8 = 16; 2 groups of 8; 2 times 8 = 16; 2 eights; 2 x 8 = 16.
Match the following: adding sentences with times / grou...: 9+9+9 = 3 x 9 = 27; seven 5s = 7 x 5 = 35; five 3s = 5 x 3 = 15; four 10s = 4 x 10 = 40; 8+8+8 = 3 x 8 = 24.
imp_items: 5 plates with 3 rotis on each plate. Write it as adding, as times and with ×, and find the total.
Write 6 + 6 + 6 + 6 with times and ×, and find the total.
Complete the table of 5 up to 5 × 6.
Make the first four numbers of the table of 10 from two tables of 5.
Arrange 12 counters in equal rows in different ways and write the facts.

title: Which Season is it?
intro: In Class 2 Maths Chapter 9, Which Season is it?, the topics are: Seasons of the Year, calendar: months, weeks and days, reading the clock: o'clock, how long does it take?, left, right and straight, east, west, north or south. Read the short notes, check every book question with the NCERT solutions, practise the important questions and then try the 30-mark sample paper. All four PDFs are free to download.
topics: Seasons of the Year
A year has five seasons — spring, summer, rainy season, autumn and winter
Calendar: Months, Weeks and Days
A calendar shows the 12 months of a year, the days of each month and the 7 days of each week
Reading the Clock: O'clock
A clock has a short hour hand and a long minute hand
How Long Does it Take?
Some things take hours, some take days, some take months, and our age is counted in years
Left, Right and Straight
We give and follow a way using left, right and straight
East, West, North or South
Face the rising sun: that is East

items: A year has five seasons — spring, summer, rainy season, autumn and winter. Each season has its own signs, clothes, food and festivals.
Five seasons in a year, in order: spring, summer, rainy season, autumn, winter
Look for the sign to name the season: flowers, sun, rain, falling leaves, cold
A calendar shows the 12 months of a year, the days of each month and the 7 days of each week. Months have 31, 30 or 28 (sometimes 29) days.
12 months, 7 days in a week
31: Jan, Mar, May, Jul, Aug, Oct, Dec · 30: Apr, Jun, Sep, Nov · Feb: 28 or 29
A clock has a short hour hand and a long minute hand. When the long hand is on 12, the short hand shows the hour: that is '__ o'clock'.
Short hand = hour hand, long hand = minute hand
Long hand on 12 → read the short hand → '__ o'clock'
Some things take hours, some take days, some take months, and our age is counted in years. We find how long by counting from the start to the end.
Short things: hours · longer: days · longer still: months · age: years
Count on from the start to the end
We give and follow a way using left, right and straight. Left and right depend on the way you are facing.
Left, right, straight = directions from where I stand
Say the turns as the walker faces, not as you see the map
Face the rising sun: that is East. West is behind you, North on your left, South on your right. A compass finds these directions.
Face the rising sun: East in front, West behind, North on the left, South on the right
East ↔ West and North ↔ South are opposites
Wrong: There are only three seasons: summer, rainy and winter. Right: The book names five: spring and autumn too
Wrong: Every month has 30 days. Right: Seven months have 31 days, four have 30, and February has 28 or 29
Wrong: The long hand shows the hour. Right: The SHORT hand shows the hour; at o'clock the long hand is always on 12
Wrong: From 11 to 5 is 5 − 11, which we cannot do, so the hours cannot be found. Right: Count on the clock: 12, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 — 6 hours (after 12 comes 1)
Wrong: Left and right never change. Right: When you turn around, what was on your left is now on your right
Wrong: North is always in front of you. Right: North is fixed: when you face the rising sun, North is on your LEFT

sol_items: Fill the number of days for the months: 31 days: Jan, Mar, May, Jul, Aug, Oct, Dec. 30 days: Apr, Jun, Sep, Nov. February: 28 (29 in a leap year).
Why do we use a calendar?: To know the day and date, and to plan school, holidays, festivals and birthdays.
Does February have the same number of days every y: No. 28 days, and 29 in a leap year.
Which months have 5 Sundays?: January, April, July, October and December (2023).
Winter vacations are in which months?: December and January
Match each activity with the time it takes: days, hours...: Hours: cooking, filling a water tank, playing, yoga. Days: knitting a sweater. Months: summer vacation, change of season.
imp_items: Leaves fall on the ground and pleasant winds blow. Which season is it?
autumn
Which season does Dussehra come in?
autumn
How many days does November have?
30 days
How many Saturdays are there in September 2023?
How many days are there in May and June together?
Short hand on 9, long hand on 12. What time is it?
9 o'clock

title: Fun at the Fair
intro: In Class 2 Maths Chapter 10, Fun at the Fair, the topics are: Notes and Coins, rupees and paise, adding money, making an amount in different ways, money left and more money needed. topics: Notes and Coins
We pay with Indian money: paper notes (₹10, ₹20, ₹50, ₹100, ₹200, ₹500) and metal coins (₹1, ₹2, ₹5, ₹10)
Rupees and Paise
A rupee can be broken into 100 paise
Adding Money
To find the total money spent or needed, we add the amounts: rupees + rupees
Making an Amount in Different Ways
One amount can be made with different notes and coins
Money Left and More Money Needed
Money given − Money spent = Money left

items: We pay with Indian money: paper notes (₹10, ₹20, ₹50, ₹100, ₹200, ₹500) and metal coins (₹1, ₹2, ₹5, ₹10). Each one shows its value in numbers and in words, so we can read how much it is worth.
₹ is the sign of the rupee
Read the number on a note or coin to know its worth
Lines on the border of a note (a different number on each note) help people who cannot see well
A rupee can be broken into 100 paise. Two 50 paise coins make ₹1; four 25 paise coins make ₹1; five 20 paise coins make ₹1.
100 paise = ₹1
Keep adding the coin until you reach 100 paise, then count the coins
To find the total money spent or needed, we add the amounts: rupees + rupees. Add the ones, then the tens, just like adding numbers.
Total → add
Add ones first, then tens; carry 1 ten when ones make 10 or more
Same price again and again → add it again and again

notes.h: Making an Amount in Different Ways
items: One amount can be made with different notes and coins. Pick notes and coins whose total is exactly the amount — there are many right ways.
Any notes and coins that add up to the amount are right
Check by adding
For the most money, choose the biggest values

notes.h: Money Left and More Money Needed
items: Money given − Money spent = Money left. When the things cost more than we have, the more money needed = cost − money we have.
Money given − Money spent = Money left
Check: spent + left = given
Cost bigger than money we have → more money needed = cost − money we have
Wrong: A bigger coin or note is always worth more. Right: Size does not tell the worth — read the number printed on it
Wrong: 50 paise is more than ₹1 because 50 is bigger than 1. Right: 100 paise make ₹1, so 50 paise is only half a rupee
Wrong: In ₹18 + ₹32 the ones make 10, so write 10 in the ones place. Right: 10 ones = 1 ten: write 0 and carry 1 ten → ₹50
Wrong: There is only one right way to make an amount. Right: Many ways are right — any set of notes and coins that adds to the amount
Wrong: 'More money needed' has the word 'more', so add. Right: It asks for the gap between the cost and the money we have — subtract: cost − money we have

sol_items: Which monument is printed on the Rs 500 note? Have you ...: The Red Fort.
A. Money for red + pink; red + green + red; blue + blue...: Red + pink = Rs 3; red + green + red = Rs 24; blue + blue + pink = Rs 11; green + yellow = Rs 30.
B. Which balloons give Rs 17, Rs 22, Rs 31?: Rs 17 = yellow + blue + red (10 + 5 + 2). Rs 22 = green + red (20 + 2). Rs 31 = green + yellow + pink (20 + 10 + 1).
C. Three differently coloured balloons for the highest ...: Green + yellow + blue = Rs 35
D. With four chances, which differently coloured balloo...: Green + yellow + blue + red = Rs 37
imp_items: Two tickets cost ₹25 each. How much for both?
How many ₹5 tickets can you buy with ₹20?
4 tickets
Ravi has ₹20. Sita has ₹5 more than Ravi. How much has Sita?
How many 10 paise coins make ₹1?
10 coins
Make ₹38 with notes and coins in one way.
₹20 + ₹10 + ₹5 + ₹2 + ₹1 = ₹38 (other ways are possible)

title: Data Handling
intro: In Class 2 Maths Chapter 11, Data Handling, the topics are: Counting from a Picture to Make a Table, reading a table: most, least, more and less, face chart: showing data with pictures, collecting our own data: asking friends, number puzzles: make the total, find the mystery number, reading numbers in new ways, count the ways and find the path, shape and picture puzzles. Read the short notes, check every book question with the NCERT solutions, practise the important questions and then try the 30-mark sample paper. All four PDFs are free to download.
topics: Counting from a Picture to Make a Table
Data is what we find out by counting
Reading a Table: Most, Least, More and Less
The biggest number in a table shows the most liked, the smallest shows the least liked
Face Chart: Showing Data with Pictures
In a face chart one face ☺ stands for one student
Collecting Our Own Data: Asking Friends
To collect our own data we ask many people the SAME question, mark each answer, write the counts in a table and then read it
Number Puzzles: Make the Total
A total can be made in many ways
Find the Mystery Number
A hidden number can be found by following the steps or by undoing them: doubling is undone by taking half
Reading Numbers in New Ways
The same number can be shown as a word (sixteen), in a mirror (backwards) or with the same digit twice (44)
Count the Ways and Find the Path
To count ways, follow every path once in an order so none is missed or counted twice; to solve a maze, try a path and go back ...
Shape and Picture Puzzles
Shape puzzles are solved by looking part by part: what is inside and outside, how many arms, which sticks make a square, which ...

notes.h: Counting from a Picture to Make a Table
items: Data is what we find out by counting. We count one kind at a time from a picture and write each number under its kind in a table.
Count one kind at a time
Tick each one as you count so nobody is counted twice
Write each number under its kind
All the numbers together = all the children counted

notes.h: Reading a Table: Most, Least, More and Less
items: The biggest number in a table shows the most liked, the smallest shows the least liked. Two numbers tell which is more than, less than or equal to the other, and adding all of them gives how many in all.
Biggest number = most
Smallest number = least
Same numbers = equal to
Add all the numbers to find how many in all

notes.h: Face Chart: Showing Data with Pictures
items: In a face chart one face ☺ stands for one student. Each kind gets its own column of faces, so the tallest column is the most and the shortest is the least.
☺ = 1 student
One column for each kind
Tallest column = most, shortest = least
Same height = equal

notes.h: Collecting Our Own Data: Asking Friends
items: To collect our own data we ask many people the SAME question, mark each answer, write the counts in a table and then read it.
Plan one clear question first
Ask each person once
Write the counts in a table
Read it like any table
A total can be made in many ways. Try, check, and change one number at a time until the total comes — and sometimes the puzzle hides a twist.
Try, check, change one number
One number up and one down keeps the total the same
Many ways can be right
A hidden number can be found by following the steps or by undoing them: doubling is undone by taking half.
Double = add the number to itself
To undo double, take half
Pieces in a line: cuts = pieces − 1
The same number can be shown as a word (sixteen), in a mirror (backwards) or with the same digit twice (44). Reading it carefully finds it.
Look for the first letter, then go across, down or up
A mirror turns each digit AND swaps their places
A two-digit number can use the same digit twice

notes.h: Count the Ways and Find the Path
items: To count ways, follow every path once in an order so none is missed or counted twice; to solve a maze, try a path and go back from dead ends.
Count ways in an order
Many ways: group them by the first step and add
In a maze mark dead ends with ✗
Shape puzzles are solved by looking part by part: what is inside and outside, how many arms, which sticks make a square, which corners make a rectangle.
Check part by part
Count small shapes first, then bigger ones
A square is also a rectangle
Wrong: Count everybody in the picture for every box. Right: Count only the children of that one kind, and each child only once
Wrong: 'Apple is less than banana' means apple has the bigger number. Right: Less than means the FIRST one has the smaller number: apple 2 is less than banana 5
Wrong: Faces can be any size or have gaps. Right: All faces the same size, one on top of the other — otherwise the tallest column may not be the most

Wrong: 'Least number of people living in a home' is the row with the fewest families. Right: Read it as: which home has the fewest people? — the first row that has at least one family (the teacher's reading; the book gives no answer)
Wrong: Every puzzle can be solved in the usual way. Right: When every try misses (29, 31), look for a twist — the 9 ball turned upside down is 6
Wrong: 6 pieces need 6 cuts. Right: After 5 cuts the last metre is already a piece — 5 cuts

sol_items: Colours table: count children wearing red, green, blue,...: Red 1, Green 3, Blue 4, Yellow 2 (10 children).
Fruits table: Banana 5, Orange 2, Apple 2, Kiwi 1, Guava 3.
Fill the mode-of-coming-to-school table from the p: On foot 8, Autorickshaw 7, Bicycle 5, Bike 2, Bus 12.
Draw faces (1 face = 1 student) for each mode in t: Columns of 8, 7, 5, 2 and 12 faces.
Games table from the picture: Cricket 8, Football 6, Pithu 5, Gilli-danda 4, Kabaddi 6.
Draw faces for each game in the chart: Columns of 8, 6, 5, 4 and 6 faces.
imp_items: A picture shows 3 cats, 5 dogs and 2 hens. Make a table.
Cats 3 · Dogs 5 · Hens 2
A bus has 9 children, 1 driver and 1 conductor. How many students are in the bus?
Table: Tea 6, Milk 4, Juice 3. How many children in all?
Vegetable table: Potato 7, Carrot 5, Peas 1. How many children like carrots?

Doll most; Car least
Table: Tea 4, Milk 4. Tea is ___ milk (more than / less than / equal to).
equal to
